summary:
The Faroe Islands are a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Criminal law and document rules extend from Denmark to the islands, while equality and family law are made locally beneath the Danish human-rights framework. Same-sex marriage was adopted locally in 2017, later than elsewhere in the Nordic region, after open friction between church and state.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was decriminalised across the Kingdom of Denmark. The age of consent was then set at 18 for male same-sex relations, and the islands did not follow Denmark's 1977 move to a gender-neutral age of 15 until 1988.

The territory's anti-discrimination provision took effect on 1 January 2007 and made the Faroe Islands the last Northern European country to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation. Anyone who publicly makes a statement that threatens, insults or degrades a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or to imprisonment for up to two years. This speech offence is the only criminal penalty touching LGBT people in the territory's legal text.

Before that law existed, violence against LGBT people went legally unaddressed. In 2006 the openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls. Police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, became mentally ill and died by suicide in 2012. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn; nowhere else had the group been attacked.

Religiously motivated opposition sits openly in Faroese politics. On 7 September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister Johanna Sigurdardottir and her partner, citing his religion. In July 2015 the same politician demanded that Pride be banned; the singer Eivor Palsdottir publicly urged people to ignore him, and his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality. He has repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the centre.

Public expression around LGBT life has been a recurring flashpoint. The first gay pride march in 2005 provoked much controversy. In June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter to the editor, 'Hvar eru vit á veg?', attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'.

Public petitioning has been used on both sides. In 2006 LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000 demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics, neither of which the territory then had; eight women in Tórshavn collected a further 2,000 signatures by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations after the assault on Rasmus Rasmussen. A petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures.
tangentialFactors:
The Faroe Islands moved later than their Nordic neighbours at each stage of the legal sequence: registered partnership and anti-discrimination protection arrived only in 2007, and marriage only in 2017, with the territory recorded as the last Northern European jurisdiction to ban sexual-orientation discrimination.

Religious argument is a sustained feature of Faroese political debate rather than a marginal position, and it has been voiced by serving parliamentarians and party leaders, including demands to restrict Pride and to move the parade out of the capital centre.

Organised public counter-mobilisation is documented alongside the hostility: petitions of 20,000 and 2,000 signatures in a territory of roughly 47,000 people, and a prominent singer publicly urging the public to disregard a call to ban Pride.

The 2005 attack on a visiting Norwegian drag troupe and the 2006 assault on a local public figure indicate that physical risk to visibly LGBT people has been recorded in the capital, and that the earlier police response was shaped by the absence of a discrimination law.
localsOnly:
Residents are covered by the local anti-discrimination provision in force since 1 January 2007, which penalises public statements that threaten, insult or degrade groups on grounds including sexual orientation with a fine or up to two years' imprisonment.

Equality and family law, including the 2017 same-sex marriage statute, are enacted by the Faroese legislature rather than by the Danish parliament, so changes to these rules are made locally.

Local advocacy organisations such as LGBT Føroyar have secured access to the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya and hold events at the Nordic House, both of which have drawn formal complaint from senior political figures.

Residents have a record of civic petitioning on both sides of the question, including the 2006 campaign for a registered-partnership law and a counter-petition of 1,262 signatures against same-sex marriage.
outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced material in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition, the procedure for changing gender markers on passports or identity documents, or whether a Danish or Faroese authority decides such applications. That question is unresolved here.

Nothing in the inventory covers entry, visa or border screening, including whether documents presenting a mismatched gender marker are examined, or any screening practice that could disclose a visitor's trans status.

The inventory does not state whether the two-year maximum penalty under the 2007 provision has ever been imposed, or how the provision is enforced in practice; the only documented enforcement failure is the police refusal in the 2006 Rasmussen case, which predated the law.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare, its availability to residents, and any waiting-list or referral rules are not sourced here.

Whether the Danish hate-crime framework or any separate aggravating provision applies in the Faroe Islands beyond the speech offence described is not established by these sources.
